Spring in the real world, in plain English

Start here

The chapter in one minute

Almost every application repeats the same non-business work: logging, security, transactions, talking to databases and other apps. A framework is a ready-made set of that work, so you write only what makes your app different.

If you remember only this

Spring is not a bag of magic tricks — it is plumbing you don't have to write. It gives your app a workshop full of parts (object management, web requests, database access, security, testing) and lets you assemble the ones you need.

Chapter 1 never asks you to code. It makes you choose Spring deliberately: know what it offers, know where it fits, and know when a plain Java class is the better answer.

01

Plumbing > business logic

In a typical app, the code for what the user wants is much smaller than the code that keeps the app alive. Frameworks supply the second part.

02

Spring is an ecosystem

Spring Core, Spring MVC, Spring Data Access and Spring testing sit inside the framework. Spring Boot, Spring Data and Spring Security are separate projects around it.

03

Inversion of control

Instead of your code creating and calling its dependencies, the framework creates and calls the parts you declare. That single flip is Spring's foundation.

04

Fit matters

Spring suits backend services, test automation, and even desktop or Android apps — but not tiny functions, locked-down security contexts, or an app that already works.

Section 1.1

Why should we use frameworks?

Because you have already solved most of your app's problems — in someone else's app.

What a framework actually is

An application framework is a set of common software functionalities that gives you a foundation to build on. It is not a library you call once; it is the skeleton your app hangs on. You don't have to use every feature it offers — you pick the parts your requirements need.

The wardrobe analogy (figure 1.1)

Image ordering a wardrobe from a DIY store. Normally you get exactly the panels and screws for that wardrobe, plus a manual. Now imagine the store instead delivers every part it sells — table legs, shelf brackets, hinges, wardrobe panels. Your wardrobe is in there, but you must find the right parts and assemble them.

That is a framework: it ships you far more capability than you will use, and it is your job to choose and assemble the right pieces into an app.

Why the idea appeared

Early applications were each unique and written from scratch. As more apps appeared, developers noticed they all had the same requirements. The book lists a few:

  • logging errors, warnings and info messages;
  • transactions, to keep data consistent (covered in chapter 13);
  • protection against the same common security vulnerabilities;
  • similar ways for applications to communicate with each other;
  • similar performance mechanisms, such as caching and data compression.

The list keeps going. The conclusion is blunt: the business logic of an app is significantly smaller than the "wheels and belts" that make its engine run — what developers call the plumbing.

What "business logic" means

The code that implements the user's expectations. "Clicking this link generates an invoice" is a use case; the code that does it is business logic. Everything else — security, logging, transactions — is supporting machinery. It is also the only part that makes two apps genuinely different.

Three reasons the trade is worth it

  1. Time and money. Reusing an implementation is cheaper than building it.
  2. Fewer bugs. Code that thousands of apps already run has been tested far more than your first draft.
  3. A community. When many developers use the same framework, someone has already hit your problem and written about it.

Here is that "iceberg" in Java. The first version is the plumbing every app needs, hand-written around four lines of real business logic. The second shows the same intent expressed with Spring annotations, which you will learn properly in chapters 4–6.

InvoiceService.javaDoing the plumbing yourself
public class InvoiceService {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(InvoiceService.class);
    private final DataSource dataSource;

    public InvoiceService(DataSource dataSource) {
        this.dataSource = dataSource;
    }

    public void createInvoice(Order order) {
        Connection connection = null;
        try {
            connection = dataSource.getConnection();
            connection.setAutoCommit(false);          // transaction: manual
            insertInvoice(connection, order);         // business logic
            insertLines(connection, order);           // business logic
            connection.commit();
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            rollbackQuietly(connection);              // transaction: manual
            log.error("Could not create invoice {}", order.id(), e); // logging: manual
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        } finally {
            closeQuietly(connection);                 // resource handling: manual
        }
    }
}

Notice what dominates: opening connections, committing, rolling back, closing, logging. The business logic is three lines. Multiply this by every service method and the iceberg becomes the whole app.

The book's warning

Using a framework is also a design and architecture decision, not just a dependency. It shapes how your app is put together — so learn the alternatives before you commit. Appendix A of the book covers software architecture in more depth.

Section 1.2

The Spring ecosystem

People say "the Spring framework", but what they really mean is a small solar system of projects, each solving one domain.

A story of transition (from the book)

The author joined a huge Java system that had grown into a "big ball of mud" over 25 years. Moving it to a modern architecture meant cleaning up the code, and the team chose Spring over Java EE because it was lighter, easier to implement and easier to maintain.

The transition was hard work — and it removed over 40% of the lines of code. That was the moment the impact of a framework became impossible to ignore.

Four parts inside the framework

PartWhat it gives youIn the book
Spring CoreThe foundation: the Spring context (which manages your object instances), aspects (which intercept and augment your methods), the Spring Expression Language (SpEL), resource management, type conversion and internationalization.Chapters 2–6
Spring MVCBuilds web applications and HTTP services in the classic servlet style.From chapter 7
Spring Data AccessTools to reach SQL databases: JDBC help, integration with ORM frameworks such as Hibernate, and transaction management.Chapters 12–14
Spring testingTools for unit and integration tests of Spring applications.Chapter 15

Picture Spring Core as the star in the middle, holding the other capabilities in orbit. Nothing works without it.

Projects around the framework

The ecosystem is larger than the framework itself. Each project is developed independently, by its own team, with its own reference documentation on spring.io/projects: Spring Boot, Spring Data, Spring Security, Spring Cloud, Spring Batch and many more. You can combine several in one app.

PROJECT

Spring Boot

Convention over configuration. Instead of configuring everything yourself, you accept a sensible default and change only what differs. Result: less code, faster starts.

PROJECT

Spring Data

A high-level layer over SQL and NoSQL databases so persistence takes a minimum of code (chapter 14).

Don't mix these two up

Spring Data Access is a module inside the framework: transactions, JDBC tools, ORM integration. Spring Data is a separate ecosystem project that layers convenience on top and spans different kinds of data sources. Similar names, different jobs.

The alternatives you should still consider

The book is careful here: there is no alternative to the whole ecosystem, but individual pieces have rivals. Jakarta EE offers CDI and EJB for object management and interceptors; Google Guice manages object instances in a container; Apache Shiro can replace Spring Security; the Play framework can replace Spring MVC; and Quarkus is a fast-maturing cloud-native option. The advice is to stay open-minded — no technology is "the one".

Section 1.2.1

Inversion of control — Spring's one big idea

Normally your code is in charge and calls its dependencies. With IoC, you hand that control to the framework, and it calls you.

Spring works on the principle of inversion of control. Through configuration, you tell the framework how to manage the code you wrote; the framework then decides when to create an instance or call a method. That is where the "inversion" comes from: the dependency controls the app, not the other way round.

The concrete piece that does this is the IoC container, which the book also calls the Spring context. You register objects with it ("make them known to Spring") and Spring then wires and manages them for you. Chapters 2–5 are entirely about it.

"Controls" is a precise word here

It means actions like creating an instance or calling a method. Spring can intercept a method and augment it — for example, log any error raised while that method runs. That interception capability is aspect-oriented programming (AOP), covered in chapter 6.

Side by side, in code

Same small app, two mindsets. First, you build the object graph by hand — every class, every constructor argument, every lifetime is your problem.

ManualWiring.javaWithout IoC
// You decide what exists, in what order, and who gets what.
var dataSource = new HikariDataSource(config);
var repository = new JdbcInvoiceRepository(dataSource);
var mailer     = new SmtpMailer("smtp.example.com", 587);
var service    = new InvoiceService(repository, mailer);

service.createInvoice(order);

Now you declare what you need and let the container assemble it. Classes announce their dependencies in a constructor; Spring supplies the rest.

ShopConfig.java + mainWith IoC
@Configuration
@ComponentScan("com.example.shop")
class ShopConfig {
}

@Service
class InvoiceService {
    private final InvoiceRepository repository;

    InvoiceService(InvoiceRepository repository) {   // Spring passes the dependency
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    public void createInvoice(Order order) {
        repository.save(Invoice.from(order));
    }
}

// Start the container once; everything declared above is wired for you.
try (var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(ShopConfig.class)) {
    var service = context.getBean(InvoiceService.class);
    service.createInvoice(order);
}

Nothing here is chapter 1 material to memorise — the book saves annotations for chapter 2. The point is the direction of control: your code stops calling the world into existence and starts describing what it needs.

Section 1.3

Where Spring actually gets used

Not only websites. The book names four real-world scenarios in which teams use Spring successfully.

1. Backend applications

A backend app runs on the server, manages data, and serves requests from client apps. Think of online banking: the mobile app and the website are clients; the backend manages accounts and transactions, stores data in databases, and talks to other backend systems.

This is where Spring's breadth pays off. Each label in the next figure is a different part of the ecosystem doing one job — and this is exactly what the rest of the book teaches.

2. Automation testing apps

Automated tests are software too. Teams build an app that validates every flow of the system under test, keep it in Git, and let a continuous integration tool such as Jenkins run it regularly and report failures. For complex systems, testing every flow by hand stops being an option.

Such a test app can be as complex as a backend: it connects to databases to verify data, messages queues to simulate scenarios, and calls REST endpoints. Spring is useful for all of that — the test frameworks themselves (Selenium, Cucumber, Gauge) sit alongside it.

3. Desktop apps & 4. Mobile apps

Desktop applications are rare now, but when you build one, the Spring context still gives you cleaner object management, plus caching or remote calls when needed. For mobile, the community project Spring for Android adds a REST client and authentication support for secured APIs.

Section 1.4

When not to use a framework

Using a tool that is too big for the job costs more energy and can give a worse result.

The chainsaw and the bread

You could cut bread with a chainsaw. It is harder, slower, more exhausting — and you may end up with breadcrumbs instead of slices. A knife is the right tool. The book lists four situations where a framework is the chainsaw.

SituationWhy the framework hurtsWhat it looks like
1. You need a tiny footprintContainers should be disposable and start fast. Every dependency adds weight and startup time.Serverless functions: tiny apps you barely control the deployment of, where a plain Java main is enough.
2. Security rules demand custom codeA public vulnerability in open source becomes public knowledge. Some organisations want the chance of exploitation near zero.Defence and governmental systems that require everything to be built in-house.
3. You'd customise everythingIf fitting the framework takes more code than writing the feature, you chose the wrong framework — or none.Components that don't fit and are patched, wrapped and overridden everywhere.
4. There's no real benefitRewriting something that already works adds risk and cost for no gain.Replacing a working setup because a new framework is popular.
The apparent contradiction, resolved

Earlier, open source was called more secure because a discovered vulnerability gets fixed publicly. Both are true. With enough time and money you can reach that standard yourself — it is simply more expensive. Most projects should use the framework; a few deliberately don't.

An avoidable mistake (from the book)

The team had ugly, hand-written JDBC everywhere. They wanted less code. The author suggested Spring's JdbcTemplate; others pushed for Hibernate because it was popular. After a proof of concept, two months of effort and a lot of stress, the team quit Hibernate and finished with JdbcTemplate — cleaner code, far fewer lines, no new framework.

The lesson: popularity is not a requirement. Ask what the change actually buys you. Jumping into it without a proof of concept is how good teams lose months.

This is what "no framework" can look like when it is the right call — the whole app, one file, no dependencies, starts instantly:

SlugFunction.javaWhen plain Java wins
import java.util.Locale;

/** A tiny function deployed in a container. A framework would only add weight. */
public final class SlugFunction {

    private SlugFunction() {
    }

    public static String apply(String title) {
        return title.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)
                    .trim()
                    .replaceAll("[^a-z0-9]+", "-")
                    .replaceAll("(^-|-$)", "");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(apply("  Spring in the Real World!  "));
        // spring-in-the-real-world
    }
}
Section 1.5

What you will be able to do after the book

The book assumes you know nothing about frameworks — and nothing about Spring.

It teaches the ecosystem, not only the core framework, and it deliberately doesn't follow a straight line: some ideas arrive early and only make sense once a few more puzzle pieces are in place. By the end you will be able to:

  • Use the Spring context and implement aspects around objects the framework manages.
  • Connect a Spring app to a database and work with persisted data.
  • Exchange data between apps over REST APIs built with Spring.
  • Build apps that use the convention-over-configuration approach.
  • Apply best practices to the standard class design of a Spring application.
  • Properly test your Spring implementations.
Companion

Every idea in this chapter, as code

Chapter 1 contains no listings of its own. These examples are written for this page so each figure has something concrete to point at — they are short, illustrative, and each one is annotated with the chapter where the book covers it properly.

The infrastructure Spring Boot removes

Figure 1.6 lists Spring Boot as "write less code to implement the app". The difference is easiest to see at the entry point: a servlet deployment needs wiring and a container; Boot needs one annotation and a main method.

ShopApplication.javaSpring Boot · ch. 7
@SpringBootApplication
public class ShopApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(ShopApplication.class, args);
    }
}

Backend: a REST endpoint (figure 1.6)

The client apps in figure 1.5 need something to call. A controller is a small class whose methods answer HTTP requests; Spring handles routing, JSON conversion and the servlet plumbing.

InvoiceController.javaSpring MVC · ch. 7
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/invoices")
public class InvoiceController {

    private final InvoiceRepository repository;

    public InvoiceController(InvoiceRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public InvoiceDto byId(@PathVariable long id) {
        return repository.findById(id)
                         .map(InvoiceDto::from)
                         .orElseThrow(() -> new ResponseStatusException(
                                 HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "No invoice " + id));
    }

    @GetMapping
    public List<InvoiceDto> byCustomer(@RequestParam long customerId) {
        return repository.findByCustomerId(customerId)
                         .stream()
                         .map(InvoiceDto::from)
                         .toList();
    }
}

Persistence: Spring Data vs Spring Data Access

The distinction from section 1.2 in one pair of examples. With Spring Data you declare an interface and Spring writes the implementation; the method name findByCustomerId is the query.

InvoiceRepository.javaSpring Data · ch. 14
public interface InvoiceRepository extends JpaRepository<Invoice, Long> {

    List<Invoice> findByCustomerId(long customerId);

    @Query("select sum(i.amount) from Invoice i where i.customerId = :customerId")
    BigDecimal totalFor(@Param("customerId") long customerId);
}

When you want the SQL in your own hands, Spring Data Access gives you the lower-level tool the book recommends for exactly that situation — JdbcTemplate, from the Hibernate story in section 1.4.

InvoiceReportDao.javaSpring Data Access · ch. 12
@Repository
public class InvoiceReportDao {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;

    public InvoiceReportDao(JdbcTemplate jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    public BigDecimal totalFor(long customerId) {
        return jdbc.queryForObject("""
                select coalesce(sum(amount), 0)
                from invoice
                where customer_id = ?
                """, BigDecimal.class, customerId);
    }
}

Notice what disappeared

Compare this with the first listing on the page. Spring opens and closes the connection, participates in the transaction, and translates SQLExceptions. You still declare the boundary with @Transactional — the book's chapter 13 subject.

InvoiceService.javaTransactions + AOP · ch. 6, 13
@Service
public class InvoiceService {

    private final InvoiceRepository repository;

    public InvoiceService(InvoiceRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    @Transactional          // commit on success, roll back on any RuntimeException
    public void createInvoice(Order order) {
        repository.save(Invoice.from(order));
    }
}

And the logging that you wrote by hand in the first example becomes one method that applies to a whole package — this is the "aspecting" from figure 1.4, where Spring intercepts methods you define.

CallLoggingAspect.javaSpring AOP · ch. 6
@Aspect
@Component
public class CallLoggingAspect {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(CallLoggingAspect.class);

    @Before("execution(* com.example.shop.service.*.*(..))")
    public void logCall(JoinPoint call) {
        log.info("Calling {}", call.getSignature().toShortString());
    }
}

Testing: the confidence Figure 1.7 describes

Spring testing boots the parts of your app a test needs and injects them, so a test reads like the production flow instead of like setup code.

InvoiceServiceTests.javaSpring testing · ch. 15
@SpringBootTest
class InvoiceServiceTests {

    @Autowired
    InvoiceService service;

    @Test
    void rejectsAnEmptyOrder() {
        var order = new Order(1L, List.of());

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.createInvoice(order))
                .isInstanceOf(IllegalArgumentException.class);
    }
}
Hands-on

Try it in ten minutes

Chapter 1 is conceptual, so the exercise is to see the plumbing exist without writing it.

  1. Create a project at start.spring.io — Maven, Java 17 or newer — and add the Spring Web dependency.
  2. Add the controller and the ShopApplication class above.
  3. Run it and open http://localhost:8080/api/invoices. Look at the startup log: the container started, found your classes, and mapped the route — you wrote none of that.
  4. Delete @RestController and restart. The route is gone. That is control sitting with the framework, not with your code.

The only dependency you need for the web part:

pom.xmlSpring Boot parent required
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
Keep it honest

After the exercise, ask the section 1.4 questions about your own project: does it deploy as a tiny container? Does it need a footprint this small? Do security rules force custom code? If the answers are "no", Spring is probably a good fit — and if the answers are "yes", you just saved a rewrite.

Recap

The chapter's summary, in plain sentences

Eight sentences worth remembering

  • A framework is a skeleton. It provides common functionalities and a foundation structure; you assemble your code onto it.
  • It saves time and bugs. Reuse beats rewriting, and widely used code has been tested by many teams.
  • The community is part of the value. Many developers understanding the same tool means your problem has probably been solved publicly.
  • Decide deliberately. Consider all possibilities — including no framework — and weigh purpose, community size and maturity.
  • Spring is an ecosystem. Spring Core, Spring MVC, Spring Data Access and Spring testing form the framework; Spring Boot, Spring Data, Spring Security and others are projects around it.
  • IoC is the foundation. The framework controls execution; you configure how your code is managed, and the Spring context is the container that does it.
  • It isn't only for websites. Backend apps, automation test apps, desktop apps and Android apps can all use Spring.
  • Sometimes you shouldn't. Tiny footprints, strict security, endless customisation, or no real benefit are all good reasons to stay with plain Java.

Four terms to carry into chapter 2

TermMeaning in one line
Business logicThe code implementing what the user actually wants; the only part that makes apps different.
PlumbingLogging, transactions, security, persistence, communication — the machinery every app needs.
IoC container / Spring contextThe part of Spring that creates, wires and manages the objects you register with it.
Convention over configurationAccept a sensible default, change only what differs — Spring Boot's core promise.
